title: A reusable 'preserve editorial intent' prompt fragment can reduce, not restore, editorial fidelity
description: Adding a generic editorial-hierarchy instruction to the Narrative prompt (the single change in the candidate) consistently shifted outputs away from the intended company-first message and toward technical orchestration, and it introduced unsupported audience/validation claims — leading to a decision not to promote the change.
audience: Prompt engineers, Narrative/Compose pipeline owners, editorial leads responsible for model-generated messaging
rationale: This experiment provides clear, source-backed evidence that a well-intentioned, reusable prompt fragment — here titled “Preserve Editorial Intent from the Synthesis.” — can backfire: candidate runs produced stable, repeatable drift (company identity subordinated, orchestration made central) and added unsupported factual claims. The result matters because it shows that adding high-level generic guidance to a production prompt can worsen, rather than improve, editorial outcomes. Gaps and uncertainty: the result is based on three runs per condition (not statistically conclusive), the model alias may map to different backends over time, and the experiment did not include variant fragment designs or story-specific examples that might behave differently.
evidence: Candidate change: inserted section “Preserve Editorial Intent from the Synthesis.” (prompt-changes/Narrative.user.prompt.diff). Narrative mean scores dropped from 6.00 to 4.00; Compose mean scores dropped from 5.67 to 3.33. All three candidate Narrative runs and all three candidate Compose runs failed criterion C (orchestration became central) and D (unsupported additions) in every run. Decision: Do not promote; production prompt restored byte-for-byte (rollback SHA-256 matched baseline).

title: A repeatable, Git-tracked experiment workflow for safe prompt changes
description: The report documents a disciplined method for evaluating prompt edits: snapshotting baseline prompts and inputs with SHA-256, reusing baseline runs to conserve calls, running controlled candidate runs that change only one prompt file, scoring outputs against a rubric with explicit promotion gates, and rolling back when criteria fail.
audience: ML/Ops engineers, engineering managers, teams governing prompt change processes
rationale: The source provides a concrete example of governance and reproducibility for prompt experimentation — including repository checks, hash verification, controlled reuse of baseline runs, a defined scoring rubric with a hard gate, and rollback verification — which is a valuable operational blueprint for teams that must change production prompts safely. Gaps and uncertainty: the experiment used only three runs per condition and lacked randomized seeds, so statistical confidence is limited; the report notes possible backend variability for the model alias.
evidence: Repository and baseline verification: commit be882989..., baseline user prompt SHA-256 475A9DB1CA0...; exact unified diff saved at prompt-changes/Narrative.user.prompt.diff. Execution: dotnet command and model gpt-5-mini used; baseline reused three prior runs. Scoring rubric with criteria A–E (0–2) and a hard promotion gate on D. Rollback verification confirmed production prompt SHA-256 matched baseline. Tests: dotnet build passed, dotnet test 165 passed.

title: Factual/editorial-restraint as a hard promotion gate: operationalizing a safety rule
description: The experiment treated factual/editorial restraint (criterion D: no unsupported audience, need, benefit, commitment, etc.) as a hard gate for promotion; candidate prompts failed this gate consistently, which alone justified rollback despite other readable/coherent outputs.
audience: Product owners, editorial governance teams, compliance and legal stakeholders involved in model-generated messaging
rationale: The report shows how an explicit, non-negotiable evaluation criterion can prevent unsafe or unsupported messaging from reaching production even when outputs are otherwise coherent and readable. This clarifies how to operationalize editorial safety in pipeline promotion decisions. Gaps and uncertainty: the report does not document alternative mitigations that might have preserved the change (e.g., more constrained wording, story-specific anchors) or whether iterative revisions could have passed the gate.
evidence: Rubric D defined as hard promotion gate: score 2 = no unsupported audience/need/benefit/commitment added. All candidate Narrative and Compose runs failed D (introducing validation intent/audience or implied commitments). Decision: Do not promote; candidate prompt not pushed, production prompt restored exactly.

title: Generic preservation guidance vs. story-specific constraints: why general prompts may encourage generic or technical drift
description: The candidate prompt added a general instruction to preserve primary message and hierarchy but contained no story-specific examples; the result was outputs that generalized the audience and emphasized orchestration, suggesting that overly generic preservation guidance can cause the model to default to technical framing instead of the intended company-level emphasis.
audience: Prompt authors, editorial designers, content strategists who craft system/user prompts
rationale: The experiment highlights a design trade-off for reusable prompt fragments: without story-level anchors, a preservation rule may cause the model to prioritize stable, high-salience technical themes (like orchestration) and to invent or generalize audiences or commitments. This matters when teams aim to maintain fine-grained editorial hierarchies across varied inputs. Gaps and uncertainty: causality is inferred (the fragment correlated with drift), but the report notes internal tension in the baseline Synthesis and possible backend/model variability, so the precise mechanism is unproven.
evidence: Candidate prompt content described as a single generic section instructing Narrative to 'identify the primary message, supporting themes, and contextual details; preserve audience scope and relative emphasis; keep technical details subordinate when Synthesis does; and retain uncertainty when the source is ambiguous.' Candidate outputs subordinated company identity and made orchestration central; they also introduced unsupported audience/validation framing. Baseline Synthesis included both company identity emphasis and a later statement calling orchestration 'central to the product direction,' which the report notes as a potential internal tension.

title: Baseline internal tension (company-first vs orchestration-first) may amplify prompt-change risk
description: The baseline Synthesis contained both a top-level company+product emphasis and a later line framing orchestration as 'central to the product direction.' The report suggests that this internal tension in the baseline content could have predisposed the model to magnify the orchestration angle when the candidate prompt attempted to preserve editorial intent.
audience: Editorial reviewers, prompt testers, Narrative content auditors
rationale: Identifying ambiguous or internally conflicted source content before applying reusable editorial constraints may be important because such tensions can be amplified by prompt changes. The report flags this as a plausible contributing factor to the observed drift, which is useful for teams designing experiments and reviewing baseline Synthesis outputs. Gaps and uncertainty: the causal link is explicitly noted as uncertain in the report ('may have reinforced the technical angle'); it is an interpretation rather than an established fact and would require targeted experiments to confirm.
evidence: Report statement: 'The baseline Synthesis pairs company identity with Compose in its top-level emphasis, but also contains a later description calling orchestration “central to the product direction.” That internal tension may have reinforced the technical angle.' Candidate runs indeed amplified orchestration and subordinated company identity, but the experiment did not isolate this baseline tension as the definitive cause.
